newsitem.title: FRANCE: Galliano stages Shanghai parade at Dior.
newsitem.headline: Galliano stages Shanghai parade at Dior.

text.p: Swashbuckling British designer John Galliano let loose his first ready-to-wear collection for the house of Christian Dior on Tuesday, drawing inspiration from opium dens, Shanghai nightclubs and 1950s babydolls.
The bobby socks, purple platform shoes and curvy suits reminiscent of the label's landmark "new look" came with micro miniskirts so short they exposed the models' underwear.
Galliano discarded blouses, replacing them with Masai necklaces of pearls or filigreed silver, while Obi bows or Japanese combs decorated hats and handbags.
Chinese-style dresses with Ming collars were the pillar of this collection, whether in pastel angora fringed with silver beads, or stretchy jacquard in candy colours like lilac and canary yellow.
There were also little strapless numbers of red or gold necktie silk with skirts sculpted from Dior's signature bow.
The collection was yet another example of the 36-year-old designer's exuberant creativity and the trouble he has with channelling it towards clothes for the shop-rack, and not the couture salon.
But in terms of sheer excitement the show was a triumph.

The evening wear was sensuous and stunning: fringed opium-den dresses or sinewy bias-cut black gowns painted with orchids and lined with plum satin. An aqua crepe de chine column swirling with floral embroidery was one of the masterpieces.
For a finale, Galliano marched out the likes of Cindy Crawford, Naomi Campbell and a brunette Claudia Schiffer in glimmering red dragon-lady outfits.

"It felt perfect. I think he made it into a piece of theatre which is what it should be," American model Kristin McNemany said after the show. "If you have talent, you should be in a couture house and if you don't, you shouldn't.
"I think John is the only one who deserves his position at this point. He's always done couture, even in his ready-to-wear," she added.
Japanese designer Issey Miyake never misses a chance to serve up up his latest innovations in fabric and dyeing techniques, and Tuesday was no exception.

Miyake, whose textiles have been exposed in fashion museums around the world, sent out creamy robes that looked as if he'd made them from paper, quilted jackets of luminescent fabrics and snowy wool felt coats as light as a feather.

But the fun came when he brushed splashy colours on tailored black gabardine and put them over bright fishnet tops, and dyed flowing kaftans like abstract artwork in fuschia, violet, emerald and turquoise.
Earlier, Dries Van Noten took the fashion crowd down the legendary Silk Road, mingling the shimmering silks of a Chinese courtesan with the rough-hewn wool of a Tibetan shepherd.
The Belgian designer married rustic quilted cotton coats with richly patterned kimono silk, drab wool kaftans with gold-embroidered scarves, or glimmering velveteen columns with alpaca jackets.

The line was long and layered as if the supermodels were getting ready for a bitter Himalayan winter, but the dreary shades were sometimes brightened. For instance, a heavy coat flapped open, revealing its stunning persimmon lining shot with gold flowers, or a burnished shawl was wound around the waist of a dark kaftan and tied with gold cord.
"The colours were magnificent and the clothes were so comfortable and free of aggression," enthused boutique-owner Maria Luisa.

"In Milan and London I saw so many shows with hard, violent, clothes. Very 1980s. But Van Noten is always true to himself: the layering, the strong ethnic flavour. It's a poetic journey, but clothes that any woman can wear."
